overview.title: Gemma's model summary and first generations with generate()
overview.subsection: 16.3.1 Text generation with the Gemma model
overview.main_topic: Reading the summary of the pretrained Gemma 3 1B CausalLM, and generating text from it with the built-in, compilable generate() method using greedy sampling
overview.central_idea: The KerasHub Gemma CausalLM bundles a 262,144-token tokenizer with a ~1-billion-parameter backbone (hidden size 1152) whose token embedding is reused as the output projection. Its built-in generate() method, compiled with a sampler such as "greedy", produces text far more coherent than the mini-GPT, but a pure pretrained model just continues text like a web document and is not yet useful.
overview.importance: This is the first time in the book the reader runs a real, production-scale LLM. The page sets up the key tension of the rest of section 16.3: scale gives fluency, but the pretraining objective alone does not give usefulness. That motivates prompting (p.511), instruction fine-tuning (p.512) and LoRA (p.514).
learning_objectives: Read a KerasHub CausalLM summary: tokenizer config, input layers, backbone and token embedding, and their shapes
Explain why the token_embedding row shows 301,989,888 parameters but the total equals the backbone's 999,885,952
Relate the parameter count to the 3.72 GB memory figure (4 bytes per float32 parameter)
Use CausalLM.compile(sampler=...) and generate(prompt, max_length=...) instead of a hand-written decoding loop
Describe what the two sample generations show: coherent, C4-like text that is not task-useful

Tied input/output embeddings from the mini-GPT build (p.498)

summary:
The page opens with the rest of `gemma_lm.summary()` (begun on p.509). The **preprocessor** contains a `gemma3_tokenizer` (`Gemma3Tokenizer`) with a **vocabulary of 262,144** tokens. The model, `"gemma3_causal_lm"`, has two `InputLayer`s, `padding_mask` and `token_ids`, both shaped `(None, None)` (batch size and sequence length are both variable). They feed a `gemma3_backbone` (`Gemma3Backbone`) with **999,885,952** parameters that outputs `(None, None, 1152)`: one 1152-dimensional vector per token. A `token_embedding` layer (`ReversibleEmbedding`) then maps those vectors to `(None, None, 262144)`, i.e. one logit per vocabulary entry for every position. It lists **301,989,888** parameters, but the total is still 999,885,952 (3.72 GB). All parameters are trainable and none are non-trainable.

The arithmetic explains the apparent double count: $262{,}144 \times 1152 = 301{,}989{,}888$, the size of the embedding matrix. That matrix lives inside the backbone and is *reused* ("reversed") as the output projection, the same weight-tying trick the mini-GPT used (p.498). So it is counted only once in the total. And $999{,}885{,}952 \times 4$ bytes $\approx 3.72$ GiB, because the model was loaded with `dtype="float32"` (p.509).

The authors then skip writing a decoding loop like Listing 16.9/16.10 (p.502–503) and use the `generate()` method that comes with the `CausalLM` class. It can be **compiled with different sampling strategies** (section 16.2). With `gemma_lm.compile(sampler="greedy")` and `max_length=40`, the prompt "A piece of advice" continues as a quote from "a former student of mine" with a stray `<blockquote>` HTML tag. "How can I make brownies?" turns into a forum-style post (`[User 0001]`, "I'm trying to make brownies for my son's birthday party…").

Two observations close the page. The output is **much more coherent** than the mini-GPT's, hard to tell apart from the C4 training data. But it is **still not that useful**: vaguely plausible text whose purpose is unclear. The model answers no question; it imitates web documents. p.511 explains why.

paragraphs.excerpt: Rather than implementing a generation routine ourselves, we can simplify our lives
paragraphs.what_it_says: Instead of writing our own generation loop, we can use the `generate()` function that belongs to the `CausalLM` class. It can be compiled with different sampling strategies, the ones explored in section 16.2.
paragraphs.what_it_means: In section 16.2 the authors wrote the autoregressive loop by hand: tokenize, predict, take the argmax at the last position, append, repeat (Listing 16.9), then a fixed-length, compiled-friendly variant (Listing 16.10). KerasHub ships that machinery ready-made. `compile()` on a CausalLM takes a `sampler` argument, a string such as `"greedy"` or a sampler object, which decides how to pick each next token from the predicted distribution. `generate()` then runs the whole loop, including tokenization and detokenization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Decoding a 1B-parameter model efficiently is non-trivial: it needs a fixed-shape buffer, a compiled loop and caching of attention keys and values. The built-in method hides this. Choosing a sampler is still the user's job, which is why the book taught sampling strategies first.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: KerasHub's generate() compiles the decoding step into the backend graph (XLA for JAX/TF) and uses a key/value cache, so each new token costs one forward pass over a single position rather than re-running the whole sequence. Listing 16.9 re-ran the whole sequence for every token.

terminology.meaning: KerasHub's high-level task model for causal (left-to-right, next-token) language modeling; it bundles a preprocessor (tokenizer) and a backbone.
The strategy used to choose the next token from the model's predicted probability distribution (greedy, random, top-K, beam, …).

p.503: Listing 16.10, the fixed-length compiled generation function.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can notice a few things right off the bat. First, the
paragraphs.what_it_says: First, the output is much more coherent than the mini-GPT's; it would be hard to tell it apart from much of the C4 training data. Second, the output still isn't that useful: the model produces vaguely plausible text, but it's unclear what you could do with it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Scale has bought fluency. The 1B-parameter model trained on about 2 trillion tokens (p.509) writes grammatical, topical English, while the mini-GPT drifted and repeated itself. But both generations read like scraps of web pages: a quotation with an HTML tag, a forum post with a user header. The brownie prompt was treated as the title of a forum thread, not as a question to answer.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This separates two properties people often conflate: *modeling text well* and *being helpful*. Pretraining optimizes the first. Getting the second takes better prompts (p.511), instruction fine-tuning (p.512) or preference tuning such as RLHF (p.519).
paragraphs.technical_idea: The artifacts in the samples (`<blockquote>`, `[User 0001]`) show the training distribution through the output. C4 is filtered web text, and greedy decoding returns the single most probable continuation under that distribution, so the most typical web-page structure comes back.

Locally and globally consistent, grammatical, on-topic text.

concepts.name: KerasHub CausalLM task
concepts.definition: A high-level KerasHub model that combines a text preprocessor (tokenizer plus packing/padding) with a Transformer backbone for next-token prediction, and provides fit(), predict() and generate().
concepts.intuition: A ready-to-use 'language model in a box': text in, next-token probabilities or generated text out.
concepts.technical: Loaded with `keras_hub.models.CausalLM.from_preset("gemma3_1b", dtype="float32")` (p.509). Its summary shows the preprocessor (tokenizer) and the functional model with inputs `token_ids` and `padding_mask`. `compile(sampler=...)` configures decoding for `generate()`.
concepts.significance: The same object is used for generation here and for instruction fine-tuning on p.513–517.
concepts.misconception: That compile(sampler=...) changes the model's weights or training. It only sets how generate() picks tokens; it can also take optimizer and loss arguments for training.

concepts.name: Greedy search (greedy decoding)
concepts.definition: A decoding strategy that picks the single most probable next token at each generation step.
concepts.intuition: Always take the locally best step; deterministic, so the same prompt gives the same output.
concepts.technical: $x_{t} = \arg\max_{v} p_\theta(v \mid x_{<t})$ repeated until `max_length`. Selected here with `sampler="greedy"`.
concepts.significance: Shows the model's single most typical continuation, which is why the outputs look like the most typical web text.
concepts.example: Both generations on this page are greedy and would be identical on every run.
concepts.misconception: Greedy decoding finds the most probable *sequence*. It does not: it maximizes each step separately. Beam search (p.508) approximates the most probable sequence better.

concepts.name: Tied (reversible) token embedding
concepts.definition: Using the same matrix both to embed input token IDs into vectors and, transposed, to project the final hidden states back to vocabulary logits.
concepts.intuition: The vector that represents a word on the way in is also the 'template' the output is compared with when deciding whether to predict that word.
concepts.technical: Embedding matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$ with $V=262{,}144$, $d=1152$. Input: $h_0 = E[\text{ids}]$; output logits: $z = h_L E^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{V}$. KerasHub's `ReversibleEmbedding` layer implements both directions.
concepts.significance: With a 262k vocabulary the embedding is 302M parameters, about 30% of the model. Tying avoids a second matrix of that size.
concepts.example: The summary lists token_embedding at 301,989,888 parameters, yet the total (999,885,952) equals the backbone alone, because the matrix is shared.
concepts.misconception: That the model has 999.9M + 302M ≈ 1.3B parameters. The summary rows overlap; the total is counted once.

concepts.name: Pretrained language model as autocomplete
concepts.definition: A model trained only to predict the next token over a large corpus; generation continues the prompt with text that is probable under that corpus distribution.
concepts.intuition: Not an assistant but a very good imitator of documents.
concepts.technical: Gemma was pretrained on ~2 trillion tokens (p.509) with the same objective as the mini-GPT.
concepts.significance: Explains why the outputs here are coherent yet unhelpful.
concepts.example: "How can I make brownies?" continues as a forum post, not a recipe.
concepts.misconception: That fluent output implies understanding of the request.

code.title: Gemma 3 1B CausalLM summary (continuation of gemma_lm.summary() from p.509)
code.what_it_does: Shows the structure of the pretrained Gemma CausalLM: the preprocessor's tokenizer, then the functional model graph from the two inputs through the backbone to the vocabulary logits.

line_explanations.explanation: The preprocessor table (its 'Preprocessor: "gemma3_causal_lm_preprocessor"' header is on p.509). It holds one layer, the Gemma 3 tokenizer, with 262,144 vocabulary entries.
Name of the Keras functional model wrapped by the CausalLM task.
Two inputs, `padding_mask` and `token_ids`, both `(None, None)`: batch size and sequence length are unspecified, so any length works. They have no parameters.
The Gemma3Backbone (embedding lookup plus all Transformer decoder blocks) takes both inputs and returns one 1152-dim hidden vector per token. Its 999,885,952 parameters include the embedding matrix.

The ReversibleEmbedding applied in reverse: hidden states times the transposed embedding matrix give 262,144 logits per position. Its 301,989,888 parameters (262,144 × 1152) are the same weights already counted in the backbone.
Totals: ~1B parameters, 3.72 GB in float32, all trainable. This is what p.514 uses to argue that full fine-tuning runs out of memory.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: integer token IDs and a 0/1 padding mask, each (batch, seq_len). Output: logits (batch, seq_len, 262144), one next-token distribution per position.
code.algorithm: Standard decoder-only Transformer: embed tokens → stack of causal self-attention + feed-forward blocks → project to vocabulary with the tied embedding.
code.theory_link: Same layout as the mini-GPT of section 16.2, including the weight-tying trick of p.498, at about 1,000× larger scale.

parameters.name: Vocab size 262,144
parameters.role: Number of distinct tokens; sets the size of the output distribution and of the embedding table.

parameters.name: Hidden size 1152
parameters.role: Width of the representation each token carries through the backbone.

pitfalls: Do not add the token_embedding row to the backbone row; the weights are shared.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written check of the numbers in the summary
V, d = 262_144, 1152
print(V * d)                    # 301989888 -> token_embedding row
N = 999_885_952
print(N * 4 / 2**30)            # ~3.72 -> 'GB' in the summary (float32)
print((N - V * d) / 1e6)        # ~697.9M parameters outside the embedding

code.title: Greedy generation with CausalLM.generate()
code.original_code:
>>> gemma_lm.compile(sampler="greedy")
>>> gemma_lm.generate("A piece of advice", max_length=40)
A piece of advice from a former student of mine:

<blockquote>"I'm not sure if you've heard of it, but I've been told that the
best way to learn
>>> gemma_lm.generate("How can I make brownies?", max_length=40)
How can I make brownies?

[User 0001]

I'm trying to make brownies for my son's birthday party. I've never made
brownies before.
code.what_it_does: Configures greedy decoding, then generates continuations of up to 40 tokens (prompt included) for two prompts.

line_explanations.explanation: `compile(sampler="greedy")` sets the decoding strategy: always pick the argmax token.

`generate()` tokenizes the prompt, runs the autoregressive loop and detokenizes. The result is the prompt followed by its continuation, here a quotation with a stray HTML `<blockquote>` tag, cut off mid-sentence when the 40-token limit is reached.
The question is continued as if it were a forum thread title: a `[User 0001]` header and a post asking for help. It is typical web text, not an answer.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a Python string prompt. Output: a string with the prompt plus generated text; total length capped at max_length tokens.
code.algorithm: Greedy autoregressive decoding: repeatedly append $\arg\max_v p(v\mid\text{tokens so far})$ until max_length (or an end token).
code.theory_link: The automated version of Listings 16.9/16.10 (p.502–503), with the sampler chosen as in section 16.2.4 (p.504).

parameters.name: sampler
parameters.role: Decoding strategy; "greedy" is deterministic. Other KerasHub samplers include random, top-K, top-P and beam.

parameters.name: max_length
parameters.role: Maximum total sequence length in tokens, prompt included, which is why outputs stop mid-sentence.

pitfalls: max_length counts the prompt tokens too, not just new tokens.
Greedy outputs are deterministic, so rerunning will not give variety; use a stochastic sampler for that.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: trying another sampler from section 16.2.4
import keras_hub
gemma_lm.compile(sampler=keras_hub.samplers.TopKSampler(k=5))
print(gemma_lm.generate("How can I make brownies?", max_length=40))

deeper.title: Why the summary seems to count the embedding twice
deeper.body: Keras prints a row for every layer called in the functional graph. `token_embedding` is a layer *owned by the backbone*: the backbone calls it in the forward direction to embed `token_ids`. The CausalLM then calls the same layer object again with `reverse=True` to compute logits. Two calls, one set of weights. The 'Total params' line deduplicates weights, so it equals the backbone count. Without tying, Gemma 3 1B would need another 302M parameters (≈1.2 GB in float32) for a separate output layer.

deeper.title: Reading the two outputs as samples of the web
deeper.body: Try to name the kind of web page each output resembles. The first looks like a blog or forum post that quotes someone (with HTML left over from crawling). The second looks like a Q&A forum (a thread title, then a numbered user's post). A pretrained LM's continuation tells you which documents in its training data your prompt most resembles. That is the idea p.511 builds on: if you want a recipe, make the prompt look like the start of a recipe.

deeper.title: Scale comparison with the mini-GPT
deeper.body: p.509 says Gemma was trained on roughly 2 trillion tokens, 2,000× the mini-GPT's training data. p.508 says reaching today's generative quality would need at least 100× more parameters and 1,000× more training steps than the mini-GPT. This page shows the result of that scale-up: same objective and architecture family, far more fluent text.

visualizations.title: Shape flow through gemma3_causal_lm
visualizations.why: The summary on this page lists the shapes: token IDs (None, None) → backbone hidden states (None, None, 1152) → logits (None, None, 262144). Here the batch is 1 and the prompt is 40 tokens long (max_length=40).

misconceptions.claim: Gemma 3 1B has about 1.3 billion parameters because the backbone and token_embedding rows add up to that.
misconceptions.correction: The token embedding is part of the backbone and is reused for output logits; the total, 999,885,952, counts it once.

misconceptions.claim: Because Gemma's output is fluent, it understands and answers the question.
misconceptions.correction: The brownie prompt was continued as a forum post. A pretrained LM predicts likely text; the book stresses that the output is 'still not that useful'.
It is the total length including the prompt, which is why the outputs are short and cut off mid-sentence.

Greedy search defined; mini-GPT output gets stuck in loops.

takeaways: Gemma 3 1B: 262,144-token vocabulary, 1152-dim hidden states, 999,885,952 parameters (3.72 GB in float32).
The token_embedding (262,144 × 1152 = 301,989,888 params) is shared between input and output, so it is not double-counted.
CausalLM.compile(sampler=...) chooses the decoding strategy; generate(prompt, max_length=...) runs the whole loop.
Pretrained Gemma is far more coherent than mini-GPT, but it continues text like a web document rather than helping.

questions.question: Using the summary, verify the token_embedding parameter count and the 3.72 GB figure for the total.
questions.explanation: The embedding holds one 1152-dim vector per vocabulary token. The model is in float32 (4 bytes per parameter), and Keras reports binary gigabytes.

questions.question: Why does the total parameter count equal the gemma3_backbone count even though token_embedding lists 301,989,888 parameters?
options: The token_embedding is frozen and so is excluded from the total
The token embedding matrix is part of the backbone and is reused to compute output logits
Keras only counts parameters of the first layer after the inputs
The 301,989,888 parameters are optimizer state, not weights
questions.answer: The token embedding matrix is part of the backbone and is reused to compute output logits
questions.explanation: ReversibleEmbedding ties input and output embeddings (as on p.498), so the shared weights are counted once. It is not frozen (non-trainable is 0), Keras counts all layers, and optimizer state is not shown in summaries.

questions.question: What does gemma_lm.compile(sampler="greedy") control, and what would change if you used a top-K sampler?
questions.answer: It sets how generate() picks each next token: greedy takes the argmax, so output is deterministic. A top-K sampler would sample randomly among the K most likely tokens, giving varied output for the same prompt.
questions.explanation: The page says generate() can be compiled with the sampling strategies explored in section 16.2 (greedy, random, top-K; p.505, p.508).

questions.question: The prompt "How can I make brownies?" produced a forum post rather than a recipe. Explain this in terms of the training objective.
questions.answer: Gemma was pretrained only to predict the next token of web text. In that data, a question like this is most often followed by a forum-style post, so greedy decoding reproduces that typical continuation instead of answering.
questions.explanation: The page notes the output resembles C4 training data but is 'still not that useful'; p.511 calls the model 'a fancy autocomplete for the internet'.

questions.question: What does the output shape (None, None, 262144) of token_embedding represent?
options: A one-hot encoding of the input tokens
Logits over the full vocabulary for every position in every sequence of the batch
The attention weights between all pairs of tokens
questions.answer: Logits over the full vocabulary for every position in every sequence of the batch
questions.explanation: Batch and length are variable (None); the last axis has one score per vocabulary entry, giving a next-token distribution after softmax. It is not an input encoding, not attention (which would be seq×seq), and not a repeated hidden state.

questions.question: Can you list which parts of the mini-GPT generation code (Listings 16.9/16.10) are now handled by generate()?
questions.answer: Tokenizing the prompt, padding to a fixed length, running the model, selecting the next token at the last position with the sampler, appending it, looping until max_length, and detokenizing.
questions.explanation: Compare p.502–503 with the one-line generate() call on this page.
